analysis.one_liner: Sets enforceable rights for people in HMOs, from emergency care to outside appeals.
analysis.headline: The bill had no cosponsors and never received a hearing or vote in any of the four committees it was sent to; it died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written a consumer's bill of rights into federal law for anyone enrolled in a managed care (HMO-style) health plan. It guaranteed direct access to obstetricians and specialists, coverage of emergency room visits without advance approval, payment for routine costs of approved clinical trials, an end to contract clauses restricting what doctors may tell patients, outside review of denied claims, and disclosure of how plans pay and monitor doctors. It applied these rules to private group and individual insurance, self-insured employer plans, Medicare managed care, Medicaid managed care, and the federal employees' plan.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly tens of millions of Americans in managed care plans in the late 1990s would have gained enforceable rights: a "prudent layperson" standard so the ER cannot deny payment for what a reasonable person thought was an emergency; standing referrals and direct access to OB/GYNs; coverage of routine costs in FDA- or NIH-approved clinical trials for people with life-threatening illness; exceptions to restrictive drug formularies when medically necessary; outside review panels for denied care; bans on discrimination based on health status, genetic makeup, disability, or sexual orientation; medical record confidentiality; and plain-language disclosures of denials, grievances, and how doctors are paid. People with serious or chronic illness, women, and those in restrictive HMOs would have benefited most.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People enrolled in HMO-style health plans

how_it_helps.text: Guaranteed emergency care without prior authorization under the 'prudent layperson' standard, so plans could not deny an ER claim because a final diagnosis turned out less serious than it seemed.
Guaranteed standing referrals to specialists, direct access to obstetricians and gynecologists without a referral, and the option for a woman to designate her OB/GYN as her primary care doctor.
Required plans to cover the routine patient costs of approved clinical trials (FDA, NIH, VA, or DoD) for enrollees with life-threatening or serious illness that standard treatment has not helped.

Banned contract 'gag' clauses restricting what doctors may tell patients, required exceptions to restrictive prescription drug formularies when medically necessary, and required independent outside review panels for appealed coverage denials.

Prohibited plans from discriminating against enrollees or providers based on health status, genetic makeup, disability, sexual orientation, or anticipated need for care, and required confidentiality of medical records.

Required a three-page annual 'health prospectus' disclosing how physicians are paid (capitation, bonuses, withholds), denial and appeal rates, patient outcomes, and how to appeal or reach regulators — giving enrollees real comparison information.

Extended all of these protections beyond private insurance to Medicare+Choice plans, Medicaid managed care, and the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program, and let states adopt rules at least as strict.

analysis.who_pays: Managed care plans and health insurers would have borne the direct cost of complying: adequate specialist networks, external review panels, quality measurement, and disclosure all cost money. Self-insured employers, whose plans were brought under the new rules by amending ERISA, would have shared the cost, and the industry's standard response — higher premiums passed to employers and individuals — is the likely channel to ordinary people. The bill offered no offsetting funding source.
analysis.who_pays_short: Insurers, HMOs, and employers funding plans

drawbacks.text: The mandates would have raised administrative and coverage costs for plans and employers, which would largely show up as higher premiums; critics argued this could price some small employers and individuals out of coverage entirely.

Nearly every substantive obligation is written as compliance with regulations 'promulgated by the Secretary,' so the actual strength of the rights would have depended entirely on future rulemaking — and the bill creates no new private right to sue a plan, leaving enforcement to federal agencies.
The nondiscrimination section bars discrimination based on sexual orientation and genetic makeup, positions well ahead of federal law in 1997 and a likely flashpoint in any committee negotiation.

Applying the rules to self-insured employer plans requires amending ERISA, the federal law that shields employer plans from most state regulation — a structural change employers and insurers had long fought to keep intact.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people the bill names — someone whose HMO denied an ER visit, a cancer patient seeking a trial, a woman told she needs a referral to see her own OB/GYN — the benefits are direct and concrete, and the outside-appeal and disclosure provisions address genuine information gaps in 1990s managed care. The honest costs are real but diffuse: higher premiums spread across all enrollees, and a design that leans on agency regulation rather than enforceable individual rights, which makes the protections hostage to whoever holds the White House. A bill this sweeping without a single cosponsor was never going to survive committee negotiation intact; a narrower version with an enforceable external appeals right would have been the stronger vehicle.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four House committees on the day it was introduced, farmed out to three subcommittees over the next month, and then simply sat — no hearing, no markup, no vote — until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Charles Schumer introduced the Health Insurance Consumer's Bill of Rights Act of 1997 on November 8, 1997, days after President Clinton's advisory commission issued its consumer bill of rights for managed care.

The Speaker referred it to four committees at once — Commerce, Education and the Workforce, Ways and Means, and Government Reform — because health insurance touches each one's jurisdiction; splitting a bill that way makes action harder, since every committee must move it forward.

Over the following month it was sent to three subcommittees (Civil Service on Nov 21, Health on Nov 24, Employer-Employee Relations on Dec 10), and the record shows no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed.
The bill ended with zero cosponsors, and the 105th Congress expired on January 3, 1999 with the bill still in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: HMOs and health insurers came out ahead: they kept operating under the pre-1997 rules, with no new mandates, no external review requirement, and no disclosure obligations. Self-insured employers also kept the full ERISA shield intact. Consumers got no new federal protections; some of the same rights (prudent layperson ER coverage, clinical trial coverage, direct OB/GYN access) reached people later through state laws and a narrower federal bill years afterward.

for.name: Rep. Charles Schumer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on November 8, 1997 as a standalone codification of the managed care consumer bill of rights; it drew no cosponsors.

for.name: President Bill Clinton
for.what_they_did: His Advisory Commission on Consumer Protection and Quality issued the Consumer Bill of Rights and Responsibilities in late 1997 and Clinton endorsed it, putting managed care protections on Congress's agenda; the bill tracks its content.

against.name: Chairs of the four referred committees
against.role: House Commerce; Education and the Workforce; Ways and Means; Government Reform and Oversight
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and referred it to subcommittees; none ever scheduled a hearing or markup, so the bill never advanced to the floor.

against.name: Health insurers and managed care trade associations
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal patient-protection mandates and defense of ERISA preemption during the 1997-98 managed care debate, arguing regulation would raise premiums.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill attracted zero cosponsors from either party, so the record shows no partisan alignment — only that support never extended beyond its Democratic sponsor.

industries.industry: Health insurers and HMOs (managed care plans)
industries.note: The bill would have imposed network adequacy, external review, disclosure, nondiscrimination, and formulary-exception requirements on every managed care plan, ending their ability to control costs through prior authorization, gag clauses, and opaque utilization review. Their cost-control methods were exactly what the bill targeted, so their interest ran against the protections.

The bill amends ERISA to require employer group health plans to comply with all the new rights, extending federal mandates to companies that self-insure precisely to escape such rules. Compliance costs would flow through to their benefits budgets.

By requiring plans to pay routine patient costs of approved trials, the bill would have removed a major barrier to patient enrollment in cancer and other serious-illness research, speeding the trials themselves.

Doctors gained from gag-clause bans, utilization review standards, external appeals, and freedom from plan interference with medical communications, but faced the plan-side burden of network adequacy and disclosure rules. On balance the bill shifts authority in the doctor-patient relationship away from insurers.
